newsitem.title: USA: Miami manager says S&P cut proves woes are severe.
newsitem.headline: Miami manager says S&P cut proves woes are severe.

text.p: Acting Miami City Manager Merrett Stierheim said the decision by Standard & Poor's Corp to lower the city's bond rating to BBB Monday is proof that drastic steps are needed to fix Miami's budget woes.

"I think it certainly reinforces the need for the city commission, the city's labor unions, the next manager, who's now been appointed, to proceed with the rehabilitation of the city's finances. We've started that process," Stierheim said.
S&P lowered its rating on Miami's general obligation debt to BBB from single-A, citing the city's "sudden fiscal decline over the last year."
The rating agency said the rating could be lowered to non-investment grade if audited results for 1996 are significantly worse than expected, or if currently proposed solutions do not materialize.

Miami has a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct 1. Stierheim has already frozen wages and cut perks. He is seeking fee increases and union employee concessions to help close the gap and has proposed other new revenue sources.

Stierheim said he believes the city can solve its budget problems and repair its credit ratings, but that would be "conditioned on all of the major players bellying up to the bar and accepting their responsibility as far as adopting new fees, new sources of revenue, prudent management and concessions from the bargaining units."

Stierheim, a former Dade County manager who heads the Greater Miami Convention and Visitors Bureau, agreed to act as city manager after City Manager Cesar Odio resigned to face federal corruption charges.
Stierheim plans to step down Nov 15.
Last week, the City Commission unanimously voted to hire Dade County Finance Director Ed Marquez as the new city manager.
Stierheim said the rating cut would probably have little immediate impact because, "We don't anticipate selling any bonds right now."
He estimated it would be 18 months to two years before the city could consider reentering the bond market.
Last month, Moody's Investors Service cut its rating on Miami general obligatio debt to Baa from single-A.
The city has obtained tax and franchise revenue prepayments from the state and a local eletric utility and is seeking a $10 million loan from Dade County to help it manage cash flow.

Stierheim also said Monday that the city's two employee pension boards had agreed to consider revising the pension contribution schedules to reflect the new wage freezes and the elimination of clost-of-living increases.
That would save the city $7 million to $9 million, he said.
